claims.text: An integrated CALPHAD, machine-learning, ab initio, and experimental-validation approach can accurately determine melting-related and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy composition space.
CALPHAD-based high-throughput calculations can efficiently explore large multicomponent HEA composition spaces.
Ab initio thermodynamic data can supplement CALPHAD calculations for the proposed melting-property model.
Iterative machine-learning updates from small-scale DSC experiments can improve the proposed thermodynamic model.
The approach is intended to apply to equiatomic and near-equiatomic alloys containing 5–35 at.% of each element.
Measurements should span temperatures from the solidus to the fully molten state.
Refined CALPHAD databases can represent phases and their enthalpic and entropic contributions.
Local atomic configurations obtained from ab initio calculations can guide refinement of the thermodynamic database.
Experimental and theoretical analysis of successful and failed alloy cases can improve a thermodynamic database.
Physically informed ab initio features combined with iterative DSC feedback systematically improve thermodynamic descriptions.
The resulting model can robustly predict melting-related properties across vast HEA composition spaces.
Predicted melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting will agree with measurements within approximately 5–10%.
The approach can determine liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
Purely experimental approaches provide incomplete coverage of the large HEA composition space or incur high experimental costs.
Purely first-principles approaches impose high computational costs.
The approach requires an adequate baseline thermodynamic database for calibration.
Predictions may become unreliable outside the composition domains represented by the CALPHAD database and machine-learning model.
Limited training data and inaccurate reference databases can cause systematic prediction errors unless corrected by targeted experiments.
DSC can measure melting temperature and fusion enthalpy, while dilatometry or in-situ diffraction can measure volume change on melting.
Consistent deviations greater than approximately 10% across sampled compositions, or failure to reproduce composition trends, would refute the framework.
